title: Fix NaN gradient of tf.math.igamma at a=1, x=0
body:
Fixes #123578

 _IgammaGrad computed partial_x = exp(-x + (a-1)*log(x) - lgamma(a)).
  
At a==1, x==0 the term (a-1)*log(x) is 0 * -inf = NaN, so the gradient of tf.math.igamma w.r.t. x is NaN there. The true derivative is d/dx igamma(1, x) = e^-x = 1. Use xlogy(a-1, x) instead, matching _BetaincGrad which already does this. Other regimes unchanged (a>1 -> 0, a<1 -> +inf, nonzero x identical). Adds IgammaGradTest.

Reproduced on tf-nightly 2.22.0-dev20260718.
author: SEPURI-SAI-KRISHNA

review_comments.body:
![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

The complementary incomplete gamma function gradient `_IgammacGrad` (defined in this file) shares the same formula and NaN gradient issue at `a=1, x=0`. Applying the same `xlogy` fix to `_IgammacGrad` and adding corresponding test coverage for `igammac` will prevent similar NaN gradient issues for `tf.math.igammac`.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The tests currently only run in V1 graph mode due to `@test_util.run_deprecated_v1` and the use of `gradients.gradients`. Using `@test_util.run_in_graph_and_eager_modes` along with `tf.GradientTape` allows testing the gradient in both graph and eager modes, which provides better coverage for TensorFlow 2.x execution paths.

```suggestion
  def _igamma_x_grad(self, a, x):
    from tensorflow.python.eager import backprop
    with backprop.GradientTape() as tape:
      tape.watch(x)
      y = math_ops.igamma(a, x)
    return self.evaluate(tape.gradient(y, x))
```

<details>
<summary>References</summary>

1. Verify that unit tests are included for any new logic, feature, or bug fix and cover edge cases across supported environments. <sup>([link](/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/master/.gemini/styleguide.md))</sup>
</details>

_IgammacGrad doesn't have its own formula it calls _IgammaGrad and negates the result (return (-igamma_grad_a, -igamma_grad_x)), so the xlogy fix already propagates to tf.math.igammac. I confirmed igammac's x-gradient at a=1, x=0 goes from NaN to the correct -1.0, and added a regression test (testIgammacGradXAtZero).
Good call  rewrote the tests to use tf.GradientTape under @test_util.run_in_graph_and_eager_modes so both execution paths are exercised.

reviews.body:
## Code Review

This pull request replaces `(a - 1) * log(x)` with `xlogy(a - 1, x)` in the gradient computation of `igamma` (`_IgammaGrad`) to prevent NaN values when `a == 1` and `x == 0`, and adds corresponding unit tests. The reviewer feedback suggests applying the same `xlogy` fix to the complementary incomplete gamma function gradient (`_IgammacGrad`) and updating the new unit tests to run in both graph and eager modes using `tf.GradientTape` instead of being restricted to V1 graph mode.

Thank you for this contribution. The fix for the NaN gradient in `tf.math.igamma` at $a=1, x=0$ looks mathematically sound and well-targeted.

### Analysis
The original formulation in `_IgammaGrad` computed `partial_x = exp(-x + (a - 1) * log(x) - lgamma(a))`.
At $a=1, x=0$, the term `(a - 1) * log(x)` evaluates to `0 * -inf = NaN`, despite the true mathematical derivative at that point being $e^{-0} = 1$.

Replacing `(a - 1) * log(x)` with `xlogy(a - 1, x)` robustly handles this edge case because `xlogy` natively maps $0 \times \log(0)$ to $0$.

### Regimes Verification
- **$a > 1, x = 0$**: `xlogy(a-1, 0)` evaluates to $-\infty$ (since $a-1 > 0$). The exponent becomes $-\infty$, and $e^{-\infty} = 0$. This is correct as $x^{a-1} = 0$ for $a > 1$.
- **$a < 1, x = 0$**: `xlogy(a-1, 0)` evaluates to $+\infty$ (since $a-1 < 0$). The exponent becomes $+\infty$, and $e^{+\infty} = +\infty$. This is correct as $x^{a-1} = \infty$ for $a < 1$.
- **$x > 0$**: `xlogy(a-1, x)` is identical to $(a-1)\log(x)$.

### Unit Tests
We verified this behavior with the following unit test:

```python
import tensorflow as tf
from absl.testing import parameterized

class IgammaGradTest(tf.test.TestCase, parameterized.TestCase):

  @parameterized.parameters(tf.float32, tf.float64)
  def testNaNEdgeCase(self, dtype):
    a = tf.constant(1.0, dtype=dtype)
    x = tf.constant(0.0, dtype=dtype)
    with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
      tape.watch(x)
      y = tf.math.igamma(a, x)
    grad = tape.gradient(y, x)
    self.assertAllClose(grad, 1.0)
```

This ensures both single and double precision backends behave consistently.

title: Fix WatchGlobalProcessInfo infinite retry on service incarnation mismatch
body:
Fix WatchGlobalProcessInfo infinite retry on service incarnation mismatch

When the coordination service restarts (e.g., after task preemption
triggers a full pod reallocation), surviving tasks hold a stale
service incarnation ID. Their WatchTasksAsync RPCs fail with
"wrong service incarnation", and the WatchGlobalProcessInfo loop
retries indefinitely because it never checks the agent error state.

Check agent.IsError() after a failed WatchTasksAsync. If the agent
has entered an unrecoverable ERROR state (set by the WatchTasksAsync
callback on incarnation mismatch), return the error instead of
retrying. Transient errors that do not trigger SetError continue
to be retried.

Validation: tested on a 256-chip (64-task) multi-host JAX workload
where a single task hit a coordination shutdown barrier timeout
(DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, 63/64 tasks reached barrier). Without the fix,
all remaining tasks entered an infinite retry loop logging "wrong
service incarnation" and hung indefinitely, requiring manual kill.
With the fix, the agent.IsError() check detected the unrecoverable
ERROR state and returned immediately, allowing all tasks to exit
cleanly via std::quick_exit(42) with no manual intervention.

title: Fix host memory leak in tf.data.Dataset.from_generator during eager execution
body:
## Bug fix: host RAM leak in `tf.data.Dataset.from_generator` (#123269)

**Reproduction:** Running `from_generator` in a loop leaks ~128 MB of host RSS over 500 iterations even after `del dataset` and `gc.collect()`. GPU VRAM is unaffected.

## Root cause

Every call to `from_generator` traces three closures via `StructuredFunctionWrapper` (`init_func`, `next_func`, `finalize_func`). During tracing those closures call `numpy_function` / `eager_py_func`, which routes through `_internal_py_func` in `script_ops.py`. There, a **strong reference** to each closure is stored:

```python
# script_ops.py – the leak
graph = ops.get_default_graph()
while True:          # walk up to outermost non-FuncGraph
    ...
graph._py_funcs_used_in_graph.append(func)   # ← accumulates forever
```

In eager mode the outermost non-FuncGraph is the **process-lifetime singleton** returned by `ops.get_default_graph()`. It is never destroyed, so `_py_funcs_used_in_graph` grows indefinitely. After 500 iterations, ~1 500 closures accumulate there (each capturing a `generator_state` object), accounting for the ~128 MB RSS growth.

## Fix

When `_internal_py_func` is called while already executing inside a `FuncGraph` (as happens during `StructuredFunctionWrapper` tracing), skip the walk-to-outermost-graph and keep the strong reference on the **FuncGraph itself**:

```python
if not isinstance(graph, func_graph.FuncGraph):
    while True:   # only walk up when NOT already in a FuncGraph
        ...
graph._py_funcs_used_in_graph.append(func)
```

The `FuncGraph`'s lifetime is tied to its `ConcreteFunction` → `StructuredFunctionWrapper` → `Dataset`. When `del dataset` runs and GC collects the chain, the `FuncGraph` is dismantled, `_py_funcs_used_in_graph` on it is released, and all three closures (and their `generator_state` captures) are freed.

In graph mode and in eager mode outside any `FuncGraph` the original behaviour is preserved unchanged.

Fixes #123269
author: DakshPrajapati-afk

review_comments.body:
![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

By introducing the `if not isinstance(graph, func_graph.FuncGraph):` guard, the `while True` loop has become entirely dead code:

1. If `graph` is a `FuncGraph`, the `if` condition is `False`, so the loop is skipped entirely, and `graph` remains the current `FuncGraph`.
2. If `graph` is not a `FuncGraph` (e.g., the default `ops.Graph`), the `if` condition is `True` and we enter the loop. However, since `graph` is not a `FuncGraph`, both `isinstance` checks inside the loop evaluate to `False`. Thus, `graph` is never updated, `graph is current_graph` is `True`, and the loop terminates immediately on the first iteration.

Therefore, we do not need to walk up the graph hierarchy in any scenario anymore. We can completely remove the loop and simplify the logic to just keeping the default graph returned by `ops.get_default_graph()`.

```suggestion
  # Keep the strong reference on the current graph (which is a FuncGraph during
  # tf.function tracing or tf.data.Dataset.from_generator, or the default Graph
  # otherwise). We do not walk up to the outermost ops.Graph to avoid memory leaks
  # in eager mode, where the outermost graph is a process-lifetime singleton and
  # would accumulate py_funcs indefinitely (GitHub #123269).
```

<details>
<summary>References</summary>

1. Flag issues only when they affect clarity or long-term maintainability. <sup>([link](/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/master/.gemini/styleguide.md))</sup>
</details>

reviews.body:
## Code Review

This pull request aims to prevent a memory leak in eager mode by avoiding walking up to the outermost ops.Graph when already inside a FuncGraph. The reviewer pointed out that the introduced conditional guard makes the subsequent loop entirely dead code, as it either gets skipped or terminates immediately on the first iteration. A simplified implementation was suggested to remove the redundant loop and directly keep the reference to the current graph.

Thank you for your contribution! This is a great fix for a memory leak issue in `tf.data.Dataset.from_generator`.

### Analysis of the Issue
The memory leak occurs because `_internal_py_func` in `script_ops.py` traverses the graph stack all the way up to the root graph (which is often the global default graph in Eager mode). It then appends the registered function to `_py_funcs_used_in_graph` on that root graph. Since the global root graph persists for the lifetime of the process, these function references (and their closures) are never garbage collected, causing memory to grow indefinitely upon repeated calls to `from_generator`.

### The Fix
By stopping the traversal and using the current default graph (which may be a `FuncGraph` or local temporary graph), we ensure that the function reference is attached to a graph that will be destroyed along with the dataset or transformation wrapper, rather than the global graph. This allows the function and its resources to be properly garbage collected.

### Verification Unit Test
Here is a unit test that can be used to verify this leak and its fix. It repeatedly creates datasets from generators and checks if the function registry in the default graph grows.

```python
import tensorflow as tf
import gc

def test_from_generator_memory_leak():
    def gen():
        yield 1.0

    # Get the default graph
    graph = tf.compat.v1.get_default_graph()
    
    # Check initial size of _py_funcs_used_in_graph
    initial_size = 0
    if hasattr(graph, "_py_funcs_used_in_graph"):
        initial_size = len(graph._py_funcs_used_in_graph)

    # Repeatedly create and destroy datasets
    for _ in range(10):
        # We use from_generator with output_signature
        ds = tf.data.Dataset.from_generator(gen, output_signature=tf.TensorSpec([], tf.float32))
        del ds
        gc.collect()

    # Check final size
    final_size = 0
    if hasattr(graph, "_py_funcs_used_in_graph"):
        final_size = len(graph._py_funcs_used_in_graph)

    print(f"Initial size: {initial_size}")
    print(f"Final size: {final_size}")
    
    assert final_size == initial_size, f"Leak detected: _py_funcs_used_in_graph size grew from {initial_size} to {final_size}"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_from_generator_memory_leak()
    print("Success: No leak detected.")
```

This test will fail (assertion error) before this fix and pass after it.

commit_messages:
Fix host memory leak in tf.data.Dataset.from_generator (GitHub #123269)

Each call to from_generator traces three closures via StructuredFunctionWrapper
(init_func, next_func, finalize_func). These closures call numpy_function /
eager_py_func, which registers each closure in _internal_py_func via:

    graph._py_funcs_used_in_graph.append(func)

where graph is the *outermost* non-FuncGraph found by walking up the graph
stack. In eager mode that outermost graph is the process-lifetime singleton
returned by ops.get_default_graph() -- it is never destroyed, so the list
grows without bound. After 500 iterations this accumulates ~1500 closures
(each capturing a generator_state), leaking ~128 MB of host RSS.

Fix: when _internal_py_func is called while already inside a FuncGraph (as
happens during StructuredFunctionWrapper tracing), keep the strong reference
on that FuncGraph rather than walking up to the global ops.Graph. The
FuncGraph's lifetime is already tied to its ConcreteFunction, which in turn
is referenced by the StructuredFunctionWrapper and the Dataset. When
`del dataset` is called and GC runs, the ConcreteFunction is freed, the
FuncGraph is dismantled, and _py_funcs_used_in_graph on it is released --
freeing all three closures and their captured generator_state objects.

In graph mode and in eager mode outside any FuncGraph the existing
walk-to-outermost-graph behaviour is preserved unchanged.

Simplify _internal_py_func graph walk per Gemini review

The elif branch for func_graph.FuncGraph inside the walk-up loop was
dead code: the guard `if not isinstance(graph, func_graph.FuncGraph)`
already ensures we only enter the loop when graph is NOT a FuncGraph,
so the elif could never be reached. Remove it.

Also tighten the comment to clarify that the _FuncGraph walk-up is
preserved specifically for TF1-style legacy graph mode.

title: Avoid grabbing the `TileAssignment` mutex in the common case.
body:
Avoid grabbing the `TileAssignment` mutex in the common case.

Before this change, many trivial accessor fuctions in `TileAssignment`
would acquire the mutex protecting the materialized array. This is
especially unfortunate for accessors like `num_dimensions()`, which can
be called in loops and which should always be able to obtain the value
cheaply (without acquiring any locks) from either `iota_` or the
materialized array.

This change makes `array_` an atomic pointer to enable it to be accessed
without locking. Accessors that can use either `iota_` or `array_` are
changed to try `iota_` by default unless obtaining the value from
`array_` is cheaper. After this change, the mutex is only acquired when
we materialize the array or access `shared_array_`.

title: [PJRT] Add support for UndonatableCommonPjRtBuffer and CommonPjRtClient::MakeUndonatable.
body:
[PJRT] Add support for UndonatableCommonPjRtBuffer and CommonPjRtClient::MakeUndonatable.

Provide a factory `MakeUndonatable` for turning an existing buffer into an `UndonatableCommonPjRtBuffer`, it consumes the input buffer and returns an equivalent hold-free buffer aliasing the same device memory. It uses CommonPjRtClient's friend access on CommonPjRtBuffer to donate the tracked buffer, snapshotting the underlying raw buffer along with its definition events to construct UndonatableCommonPjRtBuffer.

Static factory `UndonatableCommonPjRtBuffer::Create` is provided as a helper on the buffer class that delegates to `CommonPjRtClient::MakeUndonatable`. Unit tests in `undonatable_common_pjrt_buffer_test.cc` have been updated to use the factory and include null-check verification.

title: PR #45263: Allow dynamic-update-slice into an unbounded-dynamic operand dimension
body:
PR #45263: Allow dynamic-update-slice into an unbounded-dynamic operand dimension

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/45263

### Problem
`InferDynamicUpdateSliceShape` rejects a valid `dynamic-update-slice` into an **unbounded-dynamic** operand dimension.

### Root cause
```cpp
const int64_t input_dim_size = operand_shape.dimensions(dim);
...
if (update_dim_size > input_dim_size) {   // input_dim_size == kUnboundedSize (INT64_MIN) for an unbounded dim
  return InvalidArgument("Update dim size %d greater than dynamic slice dimension: %d.", ...);
}
```
For an unbounded-dynamic operand dimension, `operand_shape.dimensions(dim)` is `kUnboundedSize` (`INT64_MIN`). Any concrete static update size (e.g. `5`) then satisfies `5 > INT64_MIN` and the op is rejected with a nonsensical bound (`-9223372036854775808`). The sibling `InferDynamicSliceShape` guards the identical comparison with `!IsUnboundedDynamicSize(input_dim_size)`, and this function already handles unbounded *update* sizes just above — so unbounded operands are in scope, but the operand side is unguarded.

### Fix
Guard with `!IsUnboundedDynamicSize(input_dim_size)`, matching `InferDynamicSliceShape`.

### Verification
Static reasoning: e.g. `operand = f32[?, 10]`, `update = f32[3, 5]` is rejected today (`3 > INT64_MIN`) and accepted with the fix; operand-static-with-too-large-update still errors; both-unbounded and operand-static-with-unbounded-update are unchanged. (No local Bazel build set up — happy to add a shape-inference test.)

title: PR #45816: [XLA:GPU] Don't let rank-0 dimension-size scalars inherit op sharding
body:
PR #45816: [XLA:GPU] Don't let rank-0 dimension-size scalars inherit op sharding

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/45816

📝 Summary of Changes
Stop rank-0 dimension-size scalars from inheriting the enclosing op's sharding.

🎯 Justification
Shardy-partitioned MoE models (MaxText Mixtral, DeepSeek2, GPT-OSS) fail to compile. Their bf16 top-k routing lowers into an op that, under a tiled sharding, passes a multi-dimensional sharding onto a scalar, which is invalid and aborts compilation. This has been latent and only surfaced after this #44538

🚀 Kind of Contribution
🐛 Bug Fix

🧪 Unit Tests:
New case in `mhlo_to_hlo/tests/sharding.mlir`
Copybara import of the project:

--
e12c6475bdd83bfa3871338257b0308f925065a4 by Aleksei Nurmukhametov <anurmukh@amd.com>:

[XLA:GPU] Don't let rank-0 dimension-size scalars inherit op sharding

RemoveDynamicDimension/GetDimensionSize create a rank-0 constant to hold the
static size. The mhlo->hlo op writer applies each op's mhlo.sharding to
everything created while lowering that op, so under a rank>0 tiled sharding
the scalar picks it up and HloSharding::Validate fails. Clear the
sharding around the constant as other builder helpers do.

Merging this change closes #45816

title: Fix heap out-of-bounds write in CTC loss with empty target sequence
body:
### Summary

Fixes #123396 — a heap out-of-bounds write in the native CTC loss CPU
implementation that AddressSanitizer reports as a `bad-free` when calling
`tf.raw_ops.CTCLoss` with a minimal single-class configuration.

### Root cause

`CTCLossOp` hardcodes the blank label as `num_classes - 1`. With
`inputs` shape `[1, 1, 1]`, `num_classes == 1`, so the blank index is `0`.
A label value of `0` therefore equals the blank and is treated as a
"null/finished" label in `PopulateLPrimes`, collapsing the target to an
empty sequence. `GetLPrimeIndices` then produces `l_prime = [blank]`, so
`U = l_prime.size() == 1`.

Two initialization sites in `ctc_loss_calculator.h` assume `U >= 2` and
write outside the `U x T` (here `1 x 1`) alpha/beta matrices:

- `CalculateForwardVariables` unconditionally wrote `log_alpha->coeffRef(1, 0)`
  (row 1 of a 1-row matrix). The surrounding code already anticipated
  `U == 1` via the `l_prime.size() > 1 ? l_prime[1] : blank_index_` ternary,
  but the write itself was not guarded.
- `CalculateBackwardVariables` looped `for (int u = U - 2; u < U; ++u)`,
  starting at `u == -1` and writing `log_beta->coeffRef(-1, T - 1)`.

Both are heap out-of-bounds writes that corrupt the Eigen matrix
allocation metadata, later surfacing as the ASan `bad-free`.

### Fix

Complete the already-intended `U == 1` handling:

- Guard the second-row `log_alpha` initialization behind `if (U > 1)`.
- Clamp the `log_beta` initialization lower bound with `std::max(0, U - 2)`.

The degenerate empty-target case now computes a finite loss
(`-log P(all blanks)`) and gradient instead of corrupting the heap. The
`U > 1` path is unchanged.

### Test

Adds `testSingleClassBlankOnlyLabel` to `ctc_loss_op_test.py`, which
reproduces the exact minimal input from the issue and asserts a finite
loss and gradient of the expected shapes. Runs in both graph and eager
modes. Without the fix this test crashes the process under ASan; with it,
it passes.

### Notes

- No API or behavioral change for valid CTC inputs; only the previously
  crashing degenerate case is affected.
- CLA: signed.
author: aeldesoky

review_comments.body:
![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

Using `self.assertAllFinite` is more idiomatic in TensorFlow tests than combining `self.assertTrue`, `np.all`, and `np.isfinite`. It also provides much better error messages with the exact non-finite values and their indices if the assertion fails.

```suggestion
    self.assertAllFinite(loss_value)
    self.assertAllFinite(gradient_value)
```

Thanks! I adopted the spirit of this suggestion but not the exact API: `assertAllFinite` isn't a method on the base `test.TestCase` (`TensorFlowTestCase`) — it's only defined as a local helper inside `distributions/normal_test.py` and `distributions/special_math_test.py`, so calling `self.assertAllFinite(...)` here would raise `AttributeError`.

To get the clearer, index-level failure messages you're after while using a real base-class assertion, I switched to the `assertAllEqual(np.ones_like(x, bool), np.isfinite(x))` idiom that's already used elsewhere in the suite (e.g. `tridiagonal_solve_op_test.py`, `distributions/util_test.py`). Updated in the latest commit.

reviews.body:
## Code Review

This pull request fixes a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the CTC loss calculator (`ctc_loss_calculator.h`) when the target sequence is empty (i.e., `U == 1`). It adds safety checks during the initialization of forward and backward variables to prevent heap corruption, and introduces a regression test to verify the fix. The feedback suggests using the more idiomatic `self.assertAllFinite` assertion in the test for better readability and error reporting.

### Status
The changes look good and fix potential heap corruption issues in `CTCLossCalculator`.

### Details
-   In `CalculateForwardVariables`, the check `if (U > 1)` prevents an out-of-bounds write to `log_alpha` row 1 when the target sequence is empty (`U == 1`).
-   In `CalculateBackwardVariables`, using `std::max(0, U - 2)` prevents an out-of-bounds read/write to `log_beta` row -1.

### Notes
-   Local tests have passed. Presubmit tests showed a few unrelated failures (e.g., in ads protos or unrelated compilation units), suggesting pre-existing environment issues.
-   No additional functional fixes were needed by the agent to run the tests successfully in google3, except standard formatting and path adjustments which are expected.

commit_messages:
Fix heap out-of-bounds write in CTC loss with empty target sequence

When num_classes == 1 the only class is the blank label (index
num_classes - 1 == 0). A label value of 0 therefore collapses to an
empty target sequence, so the modified label sequence l_prime contains
only a single blank and U (l_prime.size()) == 1.

CalculateForwardVariables unconditionally wrote log_alpha(1, 0) and
CalculateBackwardVariables looped from u = U - 2 == -1, both indexing
outside the 1-row alpha/beta matrices. This heap corruption surfaced as
an AddressSanitizer bad-free (tf.raw_ops.CTCLoss, issue #123396).

Guard the second-row alpha initialization behind U > 1 and clamp the
beta initialization lower bound to 0 so the degenerate empty-target case
computes a finite loss instead of corrupting the heap. Add a regression
test covering the minimal single-class reproducer, using an
assertAllEqual on np.isfinite so a failure reports the offending
indices.

title: [IFRT] Copy serialized Cord to std::string during deserialization to avoid ASan buffer overflow
body:
[IFRT] Copy serialized Cord to std::string during deserialization to avoid ASan buffer overflow

MLIR Lexer (used by the text/assembly parser) assumes the input buffer is null-terminated. When parsing text-based StableHLO or IFRT IR during deserialization, `deserializePortableArtifact` and `ParseMlirModuleString` receive a non-null-terminated `absl::string_view` from `absl::Cord::Flatten()`. If an identifier ends exactly at the buffer boundary, the lexer reads past the end of the buffer, causing an ASan `stack-buffer-overflow`.

To fix this safely across remaining callsites, we copy the serialized data to a `std::string` to guarantee null-termination before passing it to MLIR parsing or string parsing utilities.

title: PR #45595: [XLA:GPU] Support VA remapping of parameter buffer allocations
body:
PR #45595: [XLA:GPU] Support VA remapping of parameter buffer allocations

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/45595

## 📝 Summary of Changes

This PR extends command-buffer virtual-address remapping to entry-computation parameter allocations. Parameter buffers remain caller-owned, so each execution aliases their physical memory into stable VA-reservation addresses instead of transferring ownership to the VMM allocator.

- Adds `ExecutionScope::ResolveParameterBuffer`; the base implementation returns the caller buffer, while the VA-remapping implementation installs and returns the stable reservation alias.
- Renames the `PrepareReservation` hook to `Prepare` and makes `ExecuteWithBufferAllocations` accept mutable `BufferAllocations`, allowing addresses to be restored after execution.
- Tracks per-execution parameter aliases with `RecordStepAlias`.
- Releases those aliases after every execution and rewrites remapped entries back to their caller-owned addresses before teardown and result handling. The execution-scope destructor provides cleanup for error paths.
- Adds `AddVaRemappedAllocationForTesting` and a host-only fake VMM allocator to exercise the parameter-remapping path without requiring a GPU.

This PR is stacked on #45567, **[XLA:GPU] Split command buffer VA remapping into its own allocator class**. It is part 1 of 3 splitting the former #45568 implementation into reviewable changes; #45596 adds output-buffer remapping and #45597 adds the `SKIP_PROFILED` mode.

## 🎯 Justification

`SKIP_TEMP` stabilizes only preallocated temporary buffers, but profiled command-buffer update policies also need to stabilize caller-owned parameters whose physical addresses remain constant across executions. Parameter ownership prevents allocating them directly through the command-buffer reservation.

Creating a per-execution alias gives recorded command buffers a stable VA while preserving the caller's original address and ownership. Restoring the original address after execution ensures teardown and result handling never observe a reservation address.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

✨ New Feature

## 📊 Benchmark (for Performance Improvements)

Not applicable as a standalone change. This PR adds parameter-remapping support but does not select it in a production update mode. Performance evaluation belongs to the final `SKIP_PROFILED` policy in #45597.

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

- Added host-only `gpu_executable_va_remap_allocator_test.cc` coverage using a fake VMM allocator.
- Verifies that a caller-owned parameter receives the same stable reservation address across executions.
- Verifies persistent allocation-index handling, post-execution restoration to the caller address, and release of each per-execution mapping.
- Covers cleanup behavior without requiring a GPU.

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

No standalone execution test is added because no production update mode selects parameter allocations in this PR. End-to-end selection and execution coverage is provided by the stacked `SKIP_PROFILED` change in #45597.

[XLA:GPU] Support VA remapping of parameter buffer allocations

Allow command buffer VA remapping to give stable reservation addresses
to entry-computation-parameter allocations. Parameter buffers are owned
by the caller, so they are aliased into the VA reservation with Map()
each execution instead of being allocated through it:

- GpuExecutableBufferAllocator::ExecutionScope gains a
  ResolveParameterBuffer hook (base returns the caller buffer), and
  ExecuteWithBufferAllocations now takes a mutable BufferAllocations so
  subclasses can rewrite entries after execution. The Prepare hook is
  renamed from PrepareReservation.
- GpuExecutableVaRemapAllocator records each installed alias

  rewrites the remapped BufferAllocations entries back to the
  caller-owned addresses so TearDown and result handling never see
  reservation addresses (ReleaseStepAliases; the scope destructor is a
  safety net for error paths).
- No production update mode selects parameter allocations yet
  (SKIP_TEMP remaps only preallocated temp buffers); the
  AddVaRemappedAllocationForTesting seam plus a host-only fake VMM
  allocator (gpu_executable_va_remap_allocator_test.cc) exercise the
  new path: stable reservation address across executions, persistent
  allocation indices, post-execution rewrite, and mapping release.

title: [XLA:GPU] Rewrite seeded and live carry add scans to CUB device scans.
body:
[XLA:GPU] Rewrite seeded and live carry add scans to CUB device scans.

The CUB scan rewriter only matched forward add scans with an all zero
scalar init and a dead final carry. The forms this CL matches did not
reach the reduce window rewriter's tree lowering either (it rejects
reverse scans and live carry users and fails compilation on non
scalar inits), so they lowered to sequential while loops or failed
outright, and the reverse support already plumbed to the kernel was
unreachable. By associativity, a seeded inclusive add scan is the
unseeded scan plus the broadcast seed, and its final carry is the
boundary output element. Rewrite non zero inits as one elementwise
add of the broadcast init to the CUB result, feed live final carry
users a slice of the output at the last scanned position, and match
reverse scans. With this, scans that the SPMD partitioner shards on
their scan dimension lower to per shard CUB scans instead of while
loops.

title: Properly move iota_ (`std::move(other.iota_)`) and null out other.array_ (`std::exchange(other.array_, nullptr)`) inside TileAssignment move constructor and move assignment operator.
body:
Properly move iota_ (`std::move(other.iota_)`) and null out other.array_ (`std::exchange(other.array_, nullptr)`) inside TileAssignment move constructor and move assignment operator.

When `HloSharding` is moved around and assigned over during XLA passes such as `XPrecisionRewriter` (`ReplaceInstruction`), leaving `other.array_` non-null inside the moved-from `TileAssignment` while moving out `shared_array_` causes dangling pointers and aliased deallocations upon subsequent array access or assignment. Furthermore, copying `iota_` (`std::optional<IotaTileAssignment>`) instead of moving it creates duplicate internal allocations.

Using `std::move` and `std::exchange` ensures clean transfer of pointer ownership and prevents `free(): invalid pointer` crashes.

title: [IFRT] Copy serialized Cord to std::string during deserialization to avoid ASan buffer overflow
body:
[IFRT] Copy serialized Cord to std::string during deserialization to avoid ASan buffer overflow

MLIR Lexer (used by the text/assembly parser) assumes the input buffer is null-terminated.
When parsing text-based StableHLO during deserialization (e.g. on invalid input in tests), `deserializePortableArtifact` receives a non-null-terminated `absl::string_view` from `absl::Cord::Flatten()`.
If an identifier ends exactly at the buffer boundary, the lexer reads past the end of the buffer, causing an ASan `stack-buffer-overflow`.

To fix this safely, we copy the serialized data to a `std::string` to guarantee null-termination before passing it to MLIR parsing. Since this only happens during program deserialization (non-hot path), the performance impact is expected to be low, but we will need to do a follow-up if the extra cost turns out to be too high.

title: Modify CommonPjRtClient to use ExecuteArgHold for execution arguments to support undonatable buffers.
body:
Modify CommonPjRtClient to use ExecuteArgHold for execution arguments to support undonatable buffers.

This change introduces `ExecuteArgHold` as a variant type (`std::variant<PjRtRawBufferRef, CommonPjRtBuffer::ScopedHold>`) to support execution with `UndonatableCommonPjRtBuffer`.
`UndonatableCommonPjRtBuffer` enforces lifetime via reference counting alone using `PjRtRawBufferRef` (acquired via `AcquireRawBufferRef()`) as its hold mechanism. `ExecuteArgHold` allows `CommonPjRtClient` to hold execution argument references for both buffer types. Additionally, definition events for undonatable buffers are inspected during argument preparation to propagate errors and dependencies.

title: [TF:Core] Synchronize DirectSession destructor with active Run calls to prevent UAF.
body:
[TF:Core] Synchronize DirectSession destructor with active Run calls to prevent UAF.

Use lock-free atomic reference counting (`std::atomic<int> active_runs_`) via RAII `RunScope` (`fetch_add`/`fetch_sub`) on `Run()`, `RunCallable()`, `MakeCallable()`, `PRunSetup()`, and `PRun()` execution paths to track active executions. In `DirectSession::~DirectSession()`, execute a bounded 50ms polling loop (`absl::SleepFor`) with a default 60s ceiling (configurable via `TF_SESSION_DESTRUCTOR_WAIT_SECONDS`) until `active_runs_` reaches zero before tearing down session state. This mitigates heap Use-After-Free (UAF) crashes caused by concurrent query or session cancellation.

title: PR #45422: [XLA:SE] Consolidate VMM allocator mapped allocation paths
body:
PR #45422: [XLA:SE] Consolidate VMM allocator mapped allocation paths

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/45422

Stack:

1. #45419 — reclaim tests, PA accounting, and typed overlap filters
2. #45420 — map resolution
3. #45421 — allocation-record and pending-operation state
4. #45422 — mapped allocation reuse and creation

This is the fourth and final PR in a four-part DeviceAddressVmmAllocator cleanup stack and is stacked on #45421. PR #45323 is intentionally left unchanged.

📝 Summary of Changes

- Represent the two mapped-allocation address layouts with an explicit `MappedAddressMode` request field.
- Replace separate reservation-address and separate-address reuse helpers with one `TryReuseMappedAllocation` implementation.
- Replace the corresponding creation helpers with one `CreateMappedAllocation` implementation.
- Return the tracked allocation record directly from record installation and tighten checks around mapping, retry, and pending-reclaim transitions.
- Remove redundant helpers, branches, and state cleanup made unnecessary by the unified paths.

🎯 Justification

Mapped allocation reuse and creation previously duplicated most of their logic for two address layouts. The paths could drift in budget handling, pending reclamation, and record installation despite implementing the same lifecycle. An explicit mode keeps the layout-specific decisions visible while sharing the ownership, retry, mapping, and bookkeeping logic.

🚀 Kind of Contribution

♻️ Cleanup

📊 Benchmark (for Performance Improvements)

Not applicable; this is a behavior-preserving implementation cleanup.

🧪 Unit Tests:

No new test is introduced in this layer. It is covered by the pending-reclaim and mapping tests in #45419.

- PASS at `4bafd1101e5e`: `bazel test //xla/stream_executor:device_address_vmm_allocator_test --test_output=errors`.

🧪 Execution Tests:

No new GPU execution test; this layer unifies existing allocator implementation paths.

title: PR #45567: [XLA:GPU] Split command buffer VA remapping into its own allocator class
body:
PR #45567: [XLA:GPU] Split command buffer VA remapping into its own allocator class

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/45567

## 📝 Summary of Changes

This PR separates the command-buffer virtual-address remapping implementation from `GpuExecutableBufferAllocator` into a dedicated `GpuExecutableVaRemapAllocator` subclass. It is a structural refactor of the existing `SKIP_TEMP` behavior; no functional change is intended.

- `GpuExecutableBufferAllocator` is now the common base implementation for allocation resolution and the `ALWAYS_UPDATE` policy. It also remains the runtime fallback for `SKIP_TEMP` when VA remapping is unavailable.
- `ExecutionScope` is now polymorphic and is returned as `std::unique_ptr<ExecutionScope>`. Protected hooks such as `PrepareReservation` and `AllocateTransientBuffer` provide the extension points needed by address-policy-specific subclasses.
- The new `GpuExecutableVaRemapAllocator` owns the `SKIP_TEMP` implementation:
  - per-executor remapping state and synchronization;
  - deterministic VA reservation sizing and layout;
  - VMM-backed allocation of command-buffer-referenced temporary buffers;
  - persistent allocation indices combining constants with VA-remapped temporary allocations; and
  - synchronization of pending VMM operations during allocator teardown.
- `GpuExecutableBufferAllocator::Create` selects the base allocator for `ALWAYS_UPDATE` and the VA-remapping subclass for `SKIP_TEMP`.
- GPU executable and PJRT call sites now use the factory and pointer-owned execution scopes.
- The BUILD target includes the new source/header pair and retains the direct dependencies required by both implementations.
- VMM test logging now enables both allocator translation units so existing assertions continue to observe the VA-reservation messages after the code move.

This PR is stacked on #45130, **[XLA:GPU] Update command buffers when allocation policy changes**. The follow-up policy is implemented separately in #45568.

## 🎯 Justification

The base allocator previously mixed general buffer-allocation mechanics with one specific VMM address-stability policy. Splitting those responsibilities makes the default path easier to reason about and gives additional update policies a narrow place to implement reservation, allocation, and execution behavior without further expanding the base class.

This cleanup is primarily preparation for profiled command-buffer allocation policies. Existing GPU command-buffer workloads should retain the same `ALWAYS_UPDATE` and `SKIP_TEMP` behavior.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

♻️ Cleanup

## 📊 Benchmark (for Performance Improvements)

Not applicable. This is a behavior-preserving refactor and makes no performance claim.

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

- Updated `GpuExecutableTest.CommandBufferAllocationPolicy` to construct allocators through the new factory and exercise the pointer-owned `ExecutionScope`.
- Existing assertions continue to cover the persistent-allocation sets for `ALWAYS_UPDATE` and `SKIP_TEMP`, including the non-VMM fallback path.

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

- Existing `VmmTest` command-buffer tests continue to cover the two-GEMM `SKIP_TEMP` path, VA reservation reuse, and fallback when the configured allocator does not provide VMM remapping.
- `ScopedBufferAllocatorVLog` now captures logs from `gpu_executable_va_remap_allocator.cc`, preserving the execution-test assertions whose log statements moved with the implementation.

title: Support shaped types in SimplifyArithPass
body:
Support shaped types in SimplifyArithPass

Originally the pass was written for the Fusion Emitters pipeline. Now that it
is also used for CPU block codegen, we can have shaped types as well.

This change updates SimplifyArithPass to handle shaped types (vectors and
tensors) safely across several rewrite patterns:
- In FindNarrowestValueInChain, use mlir::getElementTypeOrSelf to get the
  element type before querying bitwidths. Direct calls to
  Type::getIntOrFloatBitWidth() on ShapedType failed an MLIR assertion.
- In RewriteMinMaxFWithNaNPropagation and RewriteCmpI, construct
  DenseElementsAttr constants when operating on ShapedType operands.
- Add lit tests for shaped types and scalar NaN propagation mode in
  SimplifyArithPass.

title: The API goldens now include dunder methods defined in TensorFlow
body:
The API goldens now include dunder methods defined in TensorFlow

This allows using the goldens to generate more accurate type stubs, where
e.g. `tf.Tensor` supports binary operators and `tf.named_scope` is a context
manager.

I had to also fix two issues uncovered by this change

* `tf.Tensor` dunder methods don't always use `self`, so the name-based
  `staticmethod` heuristic added earlier misfired. I moved
  classmethod/staticmethod detection to the API generator, where we
  have access to the runtime objects.
* pybind11 docstring parsing didn't support *args, which led to
  `__exit__` having the wrong signature for some types.
* `__round__` is monkey-patched into `tf.Tensor` at import time by NumPy
  "behavior" internals, so we exclude it from the API to keep the API
  generation independent from import side-effects.

title: [XLA:GPU] Refactor DotMerger to use DotOperandDims and ShapeTracker.
body:
[XLA:GPU] Refactor DotMerger to use DotOperandDims and ShapeTracker.

This change enhances the capabilities of the DotMerger pass. Instead of relying on specific patterns like DotDecomposer's normal form, the new implementation uses `DotOperandDims` to track and categorize dimensions (Batch, Contracting, NonContracting) and `ShapeTracker` to generate the necessary transformation instructions (transpose, reshape, bitcast) to align operand shapes for merging.

Key improvements include:
-   Support for merging dots with different layouts on the shared or concatenated operands.
-   Ability to handle dots with arbitrary batch, contracting, and non-contracting dimension orders.
-   Merging of dots even when the non-shared operands have multiple non-contracting dimensions.
-   Improved handling of dependencies by merging only mutually unreachable dots within an equivalence class.
-   Simplification of consumer chains (transposes, reshapes, bitcasts) after the merged dot's output is sliced.

The equivalence classes are now built based on the shared operand's source instruction and the categorized dimensions at that source, allowing for more flexible grouping. The merging process involves transforming the operands to a common shape/layout before concatenation and then creating a single large dot. The results are then sliced and potentially transformed back to match the original dot outputs.

title: fix complex dtype byte-swap overrun in ByteSwapBuffer
body:
ByteSwapBuffer computes the number of components to swap, then ByteSwapArray walks that many words in place. On the num_of_elem == -1 path the count comes from the byte size: array_len = size / bytes_per_elem, where bytes_per_elem is the 4- or 8-byte component size, so array_len already counts every component in the buffer. For DT_COMPLEX64/DT_COMPLEX128 the code then does array_len *= 2, so ByteSwapArray swaps twice as many words as the buffer holds and reads/writes size bytes past the end. This path is taken when a cross-endian SavedModel or GraphDef is loaded on a big-endian host (ByteSwapTensorContentInNode, and the public ByteSwapTensorProto), where the dtype and tensor_content length come straight from the file, so a complex Const overruns the copy buffer.

Only double the count on the num_of_elem branch, where it is an element count that has to become a component count; the size-derived branch is already the component count. The sibling ByteSwapTensor path (which passes t->NumElements()) confirms the intended arithmetic. Added a regression test that runs ByteSwapTensorProto over both complex dtypes and checks the content round-trips without overrunning.

title: PR #44403: [XLA:CPU] onednn_threadpool: cap num_workers at n in parallel_for
body:
PR #44403: [XLA:CPU] onednn_threadpool: cap num_workers at n in parallel_for

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/44403

📝 Summary of Changes
`OneDnnThreadPool::parallel_for` (xla/backends/cpu/runtime/onednn/onednn_threadpool.h)  was passing `thread_pool_- NumThreads()` as `num_workers` regardless of `n`. Before   #42581, `Worker::Parallelize` had an entry-point clamp (`num_workers = std::min(num_work_items, num_workers)`) that silently fixed this up. #42581 replaced that clamp with a branch that triggers when `num_workers > num_work_items`:

  ```cpp
  if (num_workers > num_work_items) {
    num_partitions = ceil(num_work_items / 8);
    num_workers   = std::min(num_workers, num_partitions);
  }
  ```

  For oneDNN's small-n dispatches (reorders, packing, eltwise/softmax tiles), this collapses parallelism to ceil(n/8) cores. 
  eg: On a 56-thread host, n = 20 drops from 20 active cores to 3; n <= 8 falls through to a fully serial fallback. Multiplied across the many small primitives, this causes significant regression across multiple models when built with `build_with_onednn_async=true` and `XLA_FLAGS=--xla_cpu_experimental_onednn_custom_call=true`

  Fix
  Cap num_workers at n at the caller, matching the pattern already used in xla/backends/cpu/runtime/kernel.cc and xla/backends/cpu/runtime/convolution_lib.h: 
  ```cpp
  const size_t num_workers = std::min<size_t>(static_cast<size_t>(n),
                                              thread_pool_->NumThreads());
  ```

  With num_workers <= num_work_items, the call takes the else branch (num_partitions = num_workers) and behaves like pre-#42581. For n >= NumThreads(), the cap is a no-op and the heap/cacheline win from #42581 is fully preserved.


🎯 Justification
It fixes the significant regression (25%-60%) across multiple models run on CPU with onednn

title: [PjRt-IFRT] Reject XLA HloShardingV3 (NamedSharding) format in IFRT `HloShardingSerDes` serialization
body:
[PjRt-IFRT] Reject XLA HloShardingV3 (NamedSharding) format in IFRT `HloShardingSerDes` serialization

XLA `HloShardingV3` (NamedSharding) format is currently not version compatible across IFRT SerDes versions as the version compatibility contract has not been established around `HloShardingV3`, and `HloShardingV3` is intended to be used within the local XLA compiler. Allowing `HloShardingSerDes` to serialize `HloShardingV3` format can cause potential compatibility errors when communicating across different binary versions or using persistent artifacts such as model exports.

This change updates `HloShardingSerDes::Serialize` to explicitly reject `HloSharding` containing `HloShardingV3` format, returning an `InvalidArgumentError`.

title: [XLA:BF16_PROP] Do not propagate precision across element-type-converting bitcasts and protect bitcast operands
body:
[XLA:BF16_PROP] Do not propagate precision across element-type-converting bitcasts and protect bitcast operands

Fixes an infinite loop in BFloat16Propagation::ResolveInconsistencyOfAliasingBuffersHelper across bitcast instructions with mismatched input/output element types (e.g. bf16 <-> f32 or u32 <-> f32). Specifically:
- BFloat16Propagation::ShouldKeepPrecisionUnchanged returns true for HloOpcode::kBitcast when the input element type differs from the output element type.
- AllUsersConsumeBF16 returns true when checking a user instruction that is an HloOpcode::kBitcast whose operand expects BF16.
- Ensure only F32 values (value->shape().element_type() == F32) are inserted into values_that_must_be_kept_as_f32_ in DetermineInstructionPrecision and AdjustCalledComputationRoot, preventing F32 bitcast roots from marking aliased native BF16 operands as requiring F32.

title: Fix test failures in ragged_collective_test in JAX.
body:
Fix test failures in ragged_collective_test in JAX.

There are two problems:
* we appear to be inconsistent in what the 'memory_space' argument to DeviceMemoryAllocator actually is. As used by XLA:GPU it is an XLA memory space ID, but that is not what StreamExecutorAllocator interprets it as (a se::MemorySpace value). Work around the problem by using a MultiDeviceAllocator to adapt between the two (which is how it works at all in the BFC allocator case).
* merge "address" and "platform" allocators. The semantics of "platform" have always been intended to be what the semantics of "address" are.

title: PR #45130: [XLA:GPU] Trigger command buffers update when persistent allocations set changed.
body:
PR #45130: [XLA:GPU] Trigger command buffers update when persistent allocations set changed.

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/45130

For command buffer run, add the required processing for allowing `persistent_alloc_indices` to transition only from absent to present across execution steps and must remain unchanged once present. 

We may require this transition because the chosen of buffer allocations whose address are in `persistent_alloc_indices` might not be available from the first step, e.g, if persistent allocations are only available after several steps of profiling.  So we need to make sure that command buffer is correctly updated when `persistent_alloc_indices` is changed across steps. 


📝 Summary of Changes

- Document that `persistent_alloc_indices` may transition only from absent to
  present across execution steps and must remain unchanged once present.
- Track only whether persistent-allocation information was valid when each
  executor's command buffer was recorded, avoiding an owned vector copy and
  repeated value comparisons.
- Force a full command-buffer update in `CommandBufferThunk::Initialize` when
  persistent allocation information first becomes valid.
- In `ExecuteOnStream`, recover from a recorded/current information-validity
  mismatch by fully updating the command buffer. This covers a
  profiling-skipped update and interleaving with an older execution initialized
  before policy activation.
- Use the public `ShapedSlice` header and its direct BUILD dependency.

🎯 Justification

The persistent allocation policy controls which recorded addresses a command
buffer can safely retain. When the policy first becomes available, an
allocation-filtered update can skip a command whose allocations are now all
persistent, leaving stale addresses in the command buffer. A full update fixes
that transition.

Although the policy transition is logically one-way, executions initialized on
opposite sides of it can interleave on the shared per-executor command buffer.
An Execute-time validity check therefore forces a full update for either
recorded/current mismatch without comparing policy vectors on every step.

🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

📊 Benchmark (for Performance Improvements)

N/A. This is a correctness fix.

🧪 Unit Tests:

Extended `PersistentAllocIndicesBecomingAvailableTriggersUpdate` to verify:

- absent-to-present activation during Initialize triggers exactly one update;
- Execute recovers when the initialization update was skipped;
- an older absent-policy execution and the following present-policy execution
  each restore the correct recorded addresses when they interleave.

Also ran `GpuExecutableTest.CommandBufferAllocationPolicy`.

🧪 Execution Tests:

Ran the focused command-buffer regression and allocation-policy test with
Bazel. All seven configured GPU architecture variants of
`command_buffer_thunk_test` passed, and `gpu_executable_test` passed.
